::: {.callout-important}
## How to use this notebook
The national prediction grid (17,603 cells) was built by extracting habitat covariates from
Google Earth Engine for every cell, then pushing each cell through the fitted occupancy
model -- too heavy and too dependent on a GEE service account to run in class. Those steps
are **shown as code, not executed**. This notebook **loads the delivered prediction grid**
and computes the parts that make the method transparent live: the model-adequacy screen
(AUC), the extrapolation diagnostics (MESS + covariate coverage), the range mask, the
composite presence/absence rule, and the per-species occupied-area estimate -- so you see
exactly how a fitted model becomes a national map, and where it should *not* be trusted.
:::

# What this module does

Module 4 estimated a **community occupancy model**: a single joint fit, across all 44
mammal species simultaneously, linking eleven habitat and detection covariates to each
species' probability of occupancy ($\psi$) and detection ($p$). Every species' coefficients
are partially pooled toward a community-wide mean, so a rare species with few detections
still gets an informed estimate rather than a wild one. This module takes that fitted model
and turns it into a **map of predicted occupancy across all of Brazil**, at every point on a
regular grid, whether or not a camera was ever there.

That step is arithmetic, but trusting the result is not automatic. A model fit on forested,
protected, easily-accessed camera sites has no guarantee of applying to a remote,
deforested, roadless corner of the country it never saw. This module builds the national
maps and, in equal measure, builds the diagnostics that say where those maps can and cannot
be trusted.

## Why the community model, at the camera level

Two design choices are worth stating up front, because they shape everything that follows.

**Community over single-species.** A joint community model borrows statistical strength
across species: a rare species' habitat response is partially informed by the
community-wide pattern rather than estimated from its own thin data alone. In this dataset
the payoff is concrete -- species with too few detections to support a stable independent
fit (jaguar among them) get materially better-behaved coefficients under partial pooling, at
the cost of shrinking every species' estimate somewhat toward the community mean. The
worked example toward the end of this module works through exactly what that trade-off
looks like for jaguar.

**Camera level, not array level.** The model used here is fit at the individual camera
point (~1,100 sites), not aggregated to the coarser ~20 km survey array. The camera-level
fit has far more statistical power (roughly 18x more spatial replicates) and a smaller
share of the national grid falls outside its training envelope.

```{r auc-screen}
#| echo: true
auc <- read_d("all_species_auc_community_camera.csv")
cat("Species modelled:", nrow(auc), "\n")
cat("Median AUC:", round(median(auc$auc_camera_comm, na.rm=TRUE), 3), "\n")
cat("Species at AUC >= 0.70:", sum(auc$auc_camera_comm >= 0.70, na.rm=TRUE),
    "| below 0.70:", sum(auc$auc_camera_comm < 0.70, na.rm=TRUE), "\n")
```

# Building the prediction grid

The prediction surface is a regular grid of points at **0.2 degree spacing (~20 km)**
covering Brazil's bounding box, clipped to the landmass -- **17,603 cells**. Each cell is a
location where the fitted model is evaluated, so each needs the *same eleven covariates*
the community model was fit on, measured *exactly the same way* as at the camera sites.

That last point is the one that makes or breaks a projection: a covariate measured
differently on the grid than at the cameras is a different variable, and the model's
coefficients no longer apply. Every grid covariate is therefore extracted from the identical
Earth Engine source, with the identical definition, as its camera-site counterpart:

| Covariate | Source | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| forest, savanna, pasture, cropland % | MapBiomas Collection 10 (2024), 30 m | % of a 100 m buffer in the mapped classes |
| native vegetation % | MapBiomas Collection 10 (2024), 30 m | % of a 1 km buffer in native classes |
| mean annual temperature | WorldClim v1 BIO1 | point value (degrees C) |
| annual precipitation | WorldClim v1 BIO12 | point value (mm) |
| protected-area status | WDPA (Brazil, designated PAs) | point in a PA polygon (0/1) |
| built-up surface | JRC GHSL built-surface, 2020 | mean built-surface fraction in a 5 km buffer |
| distance to the nearest mapped road | GRIP4 global roads database | Euclidean distance-transform (m) |
| distance to the nearest water/flooded surface | MapBiomas water and flooded-forest classes | Euclidean distance-transform (m) |

The last three rows -- development, road distance, water distance -- are extracted the same
way at every one of the 17,603 grid cells as they were at the camera sites: a
distance-transform raster is built once over the relevant feature layer (roads, or the set
of water/flooded MapBiomas classes), then read off at each point. Where the transform's
search neighborhood found no target feature at all, the distance is capped at the deepest
value that *was* measured rather than left as an artificial maximum, and the cell is flagged
with a sentinel indicator so a capped value is never silently mistaken for a precisely
measured one.

Each grid covariate was verified to reproduce the camera-site values exactly where the two
overlap, so the grid and the training data are on one scale. Covariates are then standardized
with the **same means and standard deviations** used when the model was fit -- not the
grid's own -- because the coefficients are on that training scale.

```{r grid-load}
#| echo: true
grid <- read_d("national_grid_covariates_11cov.csv")
cat("Grid cells:", nrow(grid), "at 0.2 degrees (~20 km)\n")
cat("Cells with complete camera-level (11) covariates:", sum(complete.cases(
      grid[, .(forest_100m, savanna_100m, pasture_100m, cropland_100m,
               native_veg_1000m, temp_mean_C, precip_annual_mm, in_pa,
               ghsl_built_5000m, dist_road_m, dist_water_m)])), "\n")
```

## The prediction equation as a raster calculator

With covariate layers in hand, prediction is arithmetic. For species $s$ with fitted
community-model coefficients $\hat\beta_s$ and species intercept $\hat\alpha_s$, every grid
cell $i$ gets

$$\hat\psi_{is} = \text{logit}^{-1}\!\left(\hat\alpha_s + \sum_k \hat\beta_{sk}\, z_{ik}\right),
\qquad \text{logit}^{-1}(u)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-u}}$$

where $z_{ik}$ is the standardized value of covariate $k$ in cell $i$, common across all
species because it is a property of the location, not the species. Read the right-hand side
as a sequence of raster operations, the way a GIS "raster calculator" would build it one
layer at a time:

1. Take the standardized forest-cover raster; multiply every pixel by $\hat\beta_{s,\text{forest}}$.
2. Do the same for every other covariate raster and its own species-specific coefficient.
3. Add all the resulting rasters together, pixel by pixel, plus the species intercept -- this
   is the **linear predictor**, a raster on the logit scale, unbounded and hard to interpret
   directly.
4. Apply the inverse-logit function to every pixel of that raster. The output is
   $\hat\psi_s$, bounded between 0 and 1 by construction, and interpretable as a probability
   of occupancy for species $s$.

Repeating this for every one of the 44 species and summing the resulting $\hat\psi$ rasters
gives a **community richness surface** -- the expected number of species present at each
grid cell.

```{r prediction-example}
#| echo: true
psi_comm <- read_d("grid_psi_community_camera_11cov.csv")
sp_cols <- setdiff(names(psi_comm), c("sid","lon","lat","richness_camera_comm",
                                        "mess_camera_comm","extrapolating_camera_comm",
                                        "cell_area_km2","n_present_thresholded"))
cat("Community psi predictions:", nrow(psi_comm), "grid cells x", length(sp_cols), "species\n")
cat("Richness range:", round(min(psi_comm$richness_camera_comm), 3), "to",
    round(max(psi_comm$richness_camera_comm), 2), "expected species per cell\n")
```

# Should we make these predictions?

Before mapping anything, two questions decide whether a prediction is worth trusting. This
module treats them as an explicit two-layer gate, applied to every species before its map is
shown.

## Layer 1 -- do we cover the covariate space? (MESS)

Even a good model is only trustworthy where the grid's environment resembles the environment
the cameras sampled. Predicting into a novel climate, land-cover, or accessibility
combination is **extrapolation** -- the model is guessing outside its training range, and
the inverse-logit will still dutifully return a confident-looking number regardless.

**MESS** (Multivariate Environmental Similarity Surface; Elith et al. 2010) measures this at
a basic, intuitive level. For each covariate, MESS asks: does this grid cell's value sit
inside the range the cameras spanned for that covariate, or outside it -- and if outside, by
how much? Concretely, for covariate $k$ with training range $[\min_k, \max_k]$ and a cell's
percentile position $f$ within that range, the similarity score is

$$
\text{sim}_k =
\begin{cases}
f & f < 0 \text{ (below the training minimum)}\\
2f & 0 \le f \le 50\\
2(100-f) & 50 < f < 100\\
100-f & f \ge 100 \text{ (above the training maximum)}
\end{cases}
$$

A cell's overall MESS score is the **most negative** of its per-covariate similarities --
one badly out-of-range covariate is enough to flag a cell as extrapolating, even if every
other covariate matches the training data perfectly. Positive MESS means every covariate at
that cell falls within the sampled envelope; **negative MESS means at least one covariate is
outside it**, i.e. the model is extrapolating there.

```{r mess-summary}
#| echo: true
cat("Grid cells extrapolating on the 11-covariate space (MESS < 0):",
    sum(grid$extrapolating, na.rm=TRUE),
    sprintf("(%.1f%% of the grid)\n", 100*mean(grid$extrapolating, na.rm=TRUE)))
```

![Extrapolation diagnostics on the full 11-covariate space. Top-left: the MESS surface -- blue cells sit inside the sampled covariate envelope, red cells extrapolate. Top-middle: the same as a red/blue mask. Remaining panels: covariate-space biplots and histograms, grey = all grid cells, red = camera sites.](mod5_figs/mess_extrapolation_11cov.png){#fig-mess}

Roughly a third of the grid extrapolates on at least one of the eleven covariates. The
biplots make the sampling gaps concrete at a basic level: the temperature x precipitation
panel shows camera sites clustered away from the hot-wet Amazon extreme; the development x
pasture panel and the road/water distance panel show the cameras concentrated at more
accessible, closer-to-infrastructure locations than Brazil as a whole; and the forest
histogram shows sites skew far more forested than the national average. Development, road
access, and water proximity turn out to be the covariates that push the most additional
cells into extrapolation -- remote, roadless interior regions are exactly where camera
deployment is hardest, so they are also where the model has the least basis for a confident
prediction.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Read the red as a sampling to-do list
The extrapolation surface is not just a caveat -- it is a **map of where Snapshot Brasil
most needs cameras in future years**. A cell is red precisely because no current camera
samples its combination of climate, land cover, and accessibility, so the model is guessing
there. Adding deployments in those regions in coming seasons would shrink the red, convert
guesswork into genuine coverage, and make every future version of this map more
trustworthy.
:::

## Layer 2 -- is the model good enough?

A projection inherits all the weaknesses of the model behind it. If a species' occupancy
model barely distinguishes used from unused sites, projecting it just paints noise across a
country. Every species is screened with **AUC** -- the area under the ROC curve, the
probability the model ranks a truly-occupied site above an unoccupied one. AUC = 0.5 is a
coin flip; 0.7 is a common "adequate" floor; 0.8+ is good discrimination.

```{r auc-screen-2}
#| echo: true
cat("Species at AUC >= 0.70:", sum(auc$auc_camera_comm >= 0.70), "of", nrow(auc), "\n")
cat("Species below 0.70:", sum(auc$auc_camera_comm < 0.70), "\n")
lo <- auc[order(auc$auc_camera_comm)[1:5], ]
cat("Species below 0.70:", paste(lo$species, sprintf("(%.2f)", lo$auc_camera_comm), collapse=", "), "\n")
```

![Camera-level community model occupancy psi, the 39 species with AUC >= 0.70, sorted by AUC. Each panel uses its own non-linear (power-law) colour scale so that low-probability areas keep contrast rather than collapsing into a single flat colour.](mod5_figs/gallery_community_hiAUC_full.png){#fig-gallery-hiauc}

![Camera-level community model occupancy psi, the 5 species with AUC < 0.70. The model discriminates weakly for these; read these patterns as suggestive, not reliable.](mod5_figs/gallery_community_loAUC_full.png){#fig-gallery-loauc}

## Community-level summary: richness and total predicted occupancy

Now that the per-species maps above show what the model predicts for each of the 44 species
individually, two aggregate views summarize the whole assemblage at once.

**Richness** is the sum of every species' predicted psi in a cell: the expected number of
species present, gated to each species' own IUCN range mask.

![Predicted community richness across Brazil (44 species, gated to each species' own range mask).](mod5_figs/richness_and_presence_community_camera.png){#fig-richness-presence}

```{r richness-summary}
#| echo: true
cat("Richness (sum of psi) -- mean:",
    round(mean(psi_comm$richness_camera_comm), 2), ", range:",
    round(min(psi_comm$richness_camera_comm), 3), "-",
    round(max(psi_comm$richness_camera_comm), 2), "\n")
```

Richness is highest in the northwestern Amazon, declining toward the drier Caatinga and the
more developed south and coast, a gradient consistent with known patterns of mammal
diversity in Brazil.

**Total predicted occupancy** answers a related but different question: where would most
animal detections occur? Richness counts *how many species* are expected at a cell; it
treats a cell with ten species each at psi = 0.1 the same as a cell with one species at
psi = 1.0 in terms of "species present", but not in terms of how many animals a camera
there would likely photograph. Summing every species' occupancy probability directly --
extrapolated everywhere on the grid, with no range-mask gating -- gives a proxy for **total
expected detections**: a cell where a few species are highly likely to be present and many
are moderately likely contributes more to this sum than a cell with the same richness spread
thinly.

```{r detection-density}
#| echo: true
cat("Summed occupancy (total expected detections proxy) -- mean:",
    round(mean(psi_comm$richness_full_extrapolation), 2), ", range:",
    round(min(psi_comm$richness_full_extrapolation), 3), "-",
    round(max(psi_comm$richness_full_extrapolation), 2), "\n")
```

![Predicted total animal occupancy across Brazil -- the sum of all 44 species' occupancy probabilities, extrapolated nationwide. Uses a different colour scheme (inferno, non-linear) from the richness map above to avoid the two being confused at a glance -- the underlying quantity is the same sum-of-psi calculation, only the framing (total expected animal presence, not species count) differs, and this view is not gated to any range mask.](mod5_figs/detection_density_map.png){#fig-detection-density}

# From suitability to a range map

A suitability surface says "this cell's habitat suits the species". It does not say "the
species lives here" -- a jaguar's habitat model will happily light up suitable forest in a
region jaguars have never occupied. Two more steps turn a suitability surface into a range
map: clipping to the known range, and choosing a cutoff that separates "present" from
"absent".

## Range masking

Range masking is a simple step: clip each species' prediction to its **IUCN range polygon**,
the expert-drawn distribution, so predicted presence outside the known range is removed.
This reuses the range-map exercise from Module 2.2 directly -- the same polygons, the same
species-to-polygon crosswalk, applied here as a spatial mask rather than re-derived.

Every one of the 44 modelled species has an IUCN polygon (three needed a taxonomic-synonym
crosswalk -- *Dicotyles tajacu* -> *Pecari tajacu*, *Subulo gouazoubira* -> *Mazama
gouazoubira*, *Passalites nemorivagus* -> *Mazama nemorivaga*). The one exception is the
**Wild Boar** (*Sus scrofa*), non-native to Brazil with no meaningful native-range polygon
here; it is projected without a range mask and flagged as an introduced-species special
case.

The mask is deliberately simple -- a spatial clip -- because the ecological judgment (which
out-of-range detections to keep vs. treat as structural zeros) was already made in the
Module 2.2 / Gate 4 exercise. Here it is only applied.

## Choosing a threshold

The final product many people want is a yes/no range map, which means turning the continuous
psi into presence/absence at some cutoff. The cutoff is a genuine choice with real
consequences: too low and the map floods with false presence; too high and it misses real
occurrences. There is no cutoff that is simultaneously "correct" for every purpose -- a
conservation planner wanting to avoid missing any occupied site and a modeler wanting a
clean, uncluttered range map would reasonably choose different thresholds.

This module uses the **maximize-sensitivity-plus-specificity** threshold (the Youden point
on the ROC curve): the psi value that best separates observed presence from absence in the
training data, in the sense of maximizing (sensitivity + specificity - 1) across every
possible cutoff. It is a principled default because it does not require picking an
arbitrary round number like 0.5, and it weighs the two error types -- missing a real
occurrence, and falsely claiming one -- equally rather than favoring one silently.

```{r thresholds}
#| echo: true
cat("Median Youden threshold across all 44 species:", round(median(auc$thr_camera_comm), 3), "\n")
cat("Threshold range:", round(min(auc$thr_camera_comm), 3), "-", round(max(auc$thr_camera_comm), 3), "\n")
```

Thresholds vary widely across species -- a common, widespread species with a naturally high
average psi has a much higher optimal cutoff than a rare, patchily-detected one. There is no
single number that works for every species, which is why the threshold is computed
separately for each.

**The rule -- present or absent, two outcomes.** Every grid cell gets exactly one of two
labels for each species:

$$
\textbf{present} = \hat\psi \ge \text{threshold, and in the species' IUCN range}
$$
$$
\textbf{absent} = \text{everything else -- below threshold, or outside the species' range}
$$

Out-of-range cells are folded into **absent** rather than carrying a separate "not assessed"
label: the model's covariate-coverage diagnostics (the MESS check above) already flag which
*regions of the grid* are extrapolation-prone, so the range maps below stay a clean
present/absent picture rather than a three-way classification with a large grey category.

```{r status-summary}
#| echo: true
status_cam <- read_d("grid_status_community_camera_11cov.csv")
species_cols <- setdiff(names(status_cam), "sid")
pct_present <- mean(sapply(status_cam[, ..species_cols], function(x) mean(x==1)))
cat("Average share of grid cells labeled 'present', across all 44 species:",
    sprintf("%.1f%%\n", 100*pct_present))
```

## From a range map to an occupied-area estimate

Once every cell carries a present/absent label, a natural next question is: how much area
does each species actually occupy? Simply counting grid cells would undercount toward the
poles and overcount near the equator, because a 0.2-degree cell is not a fixed physical area
-- longitude lines converge toward the poles, so a cell spans less ground area the further
it sits from the equator. Each cell's area is computed from its center latitude using the
standard spherical formula for a graticule cell:

$$
A(\text{lat}) = R^2 \, \Delta\lambda \, \bigl(\sin(\text{lat}_2) - \sin(\text{lat}_1)\bigr)
$$

where $R$ is Earth's radius, $\Delta\lambda$ is the cell's longitudinal width in radians, and
$\text{lat}_1$, $\text{lat}_2$ are the cell's south and north edges. Summing this area over
every cell labeled **present** gives each species' estimated occupied area in Brazil.

```{r occupied-area}
#| echo: true
area_tbl <- read_d("species_occupied_area_camera_comm.csv")
cat("Total grid area (sanity check against Brazil's known area, ~8.51M km^2):",
    round(sum(psi_comm$cell_area_km2)/1e6, 2), "million km^2\n")
top5 <- area_tbl[order(-area_tbl$occupied_area_km2)][1:5]
cat("Largest occupied areas:\n")
for (i in 1:5) cat(" ", top5$species[i], "--", round(top5$occupied_area_km2[i]/1e6, 2), "million km^2\n")
jag_row <- area_tbl[area_tbl$species == "Panthera onca"]
cat("Jaguar occupied area:", round(jag_row$occupied_area_km2/1e6, 3), "million km^2 (",
    sprintf("%.0f%%", 100*jag_row$pct_inrange_occupied), "of its IUCN range area)\n")
```

![Estimated area occupied in Brazil, top 15 species, cell area weighted by latitude.](mod5_figs/species_occupied_area_top15.png){#fig-occupied-area}

The occupied-area estimate inherits the threshold choice above -- it depends on the
species-specific cutoff chosen there. It is **not** a population estimate -- occupancy
answers "where", not "how many" -- turning an occupied-area figure into a number of
individuals requires an independent density estimate, which this dataset (unmarked
detections, no individually-identified animals) cannot supply on its own.

## Range maps for the well-supported species

Putting the present/absent rule on the map, for every species whose model clears the
AUC >= 0.70 bar, turns the individual psi surfaces above into range maps proper.

![Range maps (present / absent) for the 39 species with AUC >= 0.70, sorted by AUC. Gold = present (psi above the species' own Youden threshold and inside its IUCN range); blue = absent, which includes both assessed cells below threshold and cells outside the species' range.](mod5_figs/rangemap_community_hiAUC_full.png){#fig-rangemap-hiauc}

The present (gold) area differs species to species with each species' own IUCN range
polygon and threshold -- so a wide-ranging habitat generalist (e.g. Crab-eating Fox, Puma)
covers far more of the map than a narrow-range endemic (e.g. Rock Cavy, confined to the
Caatinga). A cell being labeled "absent" folds together two different reasons (outside the
species' range, or inside the range but below its detection threshold) rather than
distinguishing them -- a simplification chosen deliberately here to keep the map a clean
two-colour picture rather than introducing a third, harder-to-interpret category.

# Deep dive: what partial pooling does for jaguar

Jaguar is a useful worked example because it sits at the point where the community model's
main benefit -- borrowing statistical strength across species -- matters most: a large,
wide-ranging, but comparatively rarely-detected species relative to Snapshot Brasil's
smaller, more abundant mammals.

```{r jaguar-numbers}
#| echo: true
jag_auc <- auc[auc$species == "Panthera onca", ]
cat("Jaguar community-model AUC:", round(jag_auc$auc_camera_comm, 3), "\n")
cat("Jaguar Youden threshold:", round(jag_auc$thr_camera_comm, 3), "\n")
jag_hyp <- read_d("community_lpsi_camera_11cov_v5.csv")
jag_row <- jag_hyp[jag_hyp$species == "Panthera onca", ]
cat("Jaguar species intercept (lpsi, logit scale):", round(jag_row$lpsi, 2),
    "+/-", round(jag_row$lpsi_sd, 2), "\n")
```

![Jaguar occupancy probability across Brazil: an independent single-species fit (left) versus the community model used in this module (right), both at the camera level with the same core covariates. Non-linear (power-law) colour scale, own scale per panel.](mod5_figs/jaguar_deep_dive.png){#fig-jaguar-deepdive}

The two maps agree on the broad pattern -- jaguar occupancy concentrated in the
northwestern Amazon and scattered remnant patches further south and east -- but the
community model's surface is visibly more conservative (lower average psi, tighter spatial
concentration) than the independent fit. That difference is exactly what partial pooling is
supposed to do: with relatively few jaguar detections to work with, an independent model's
habitat coefficients are estimated almost entirely from jaguar's own thin data and can swing
to extreme values in either direction; the community model instead pulls jaguar's
coefficients toward the assemblage-wide pattern, trading away some of jaguar-specific detail
for a more stable, less noise-driven estimate.

## The coefficients behind the difference

The two maps above are each built from one set of numbers -- the jaguar-specific
intercept and habitat coefficients plugged into the raster-calculator formula from earlier
in this module. Here they are side by side, exactly as used, with no measure of uncertainty
attached (see the community model's full coefficient table, `community_species_betas_camera_11cov_v5.csv`,
for the credible intervals behind the community-model column).

```{r jaguar-coefs}
#| echo: true
jc <- read_d("jaguar_deepdive_coefficients_simple.csv")
knitr::kable(jc, digits = 3,
  caption = "Jaguar coefficients used to build each map. 'Community' = this module's community model (11 covariates). 'Independent' = the single-species fit from Module 3, which predates three covariates (ghsl_built_5000m, dist_road_m, dist_water_m) being added to the covariate set -- its map is built from 9 covariates plus intercept, not 11.")
```

Two patterns are visible directly in these numbers:

1. **Pasture and cropland move the most.** The independent model's pasture ($-1.00$) and
   cropland ($-0.63$) coefficients -- estimated almost entirely from jaguar's own sparse
   detections in those land covers -- shrink toward zero in the community model ($-0.09$
   and $+0.05$). These are exactly the covariates where jaguar has the least direct data
   (jaguar is rarely detected in pasture or cropland at all), so the community-wide pattern
   dominates the community-model coefficient.
2. **Temperature moves the other direction.** Jaguar's temperature coefficient is larger in
   the community model ($3.97$) than the independent model ($1.89$) -- partial pooling does
   not uniformly shrink every coefficient toward zero, it moves each one toward the
   community's estimate of the relationship, which for temperature reinforces rather than
   dilutes jaguar's own signal.

This is a real trade-off, not a free upgrade. Where jaguar's true habitat relationships
genuinely differ from the rest of the community -- plausible for a wide-ranging apex
predator with different area requirements than the smaller, more common species that
dominate the community-wide average -- pooling can understate jaguar's real habitat
specificity. The right way to read the jaguar map in this module is as the more
statistically defensible choice given the data actually available, not as a claim that it
has resolved every open question about jaguar habitat use in Brazil.

# Takeaways

1. **Projection is arithmetic; trust is the hard part.** Turning a fitted community
   occupancy model into a national map is a raster calculation, repeated once per species
   and summed for richness. The work of this module is the two-layer gate around it -- is
   the model good enough (AUC), and do we cover the covariate space (MESS) -- plus the
   range mask and threshold.
2. **Flag, don't hide, weak predictions.** Every map ships with its AUC, and every cell
   carries a present/absent label built from that species' own threshold and range mask.
3. **Partial pooling changes individual species' maps, not just their standard errors.**
   The jaguar deep dive shows a community fit can meaningfully reshape a data-poor
   species' predicted surface relative to an independent single-species fit -- a real
   trade-off between borrowed strength and species-specific detail, not a strictly free
   improvement.
4. **Occupied area is not population size.** Turning a range map into a km^2 figure per
   species is a straightforward area calculation once the present/absent labels exist, but
   it answers "where", not "how many" -- a genuine population estimate needs an independent
   density relationship this dataset cannot supply on its own.
5. **The gaps in coverage are themselves useful.** Roughly a third of the country falls
   outside the sampled covariate envelope once accessibility (road and water distance,
   development) is included alongside habitat and climate -- a map of where future camera
   deployments would do the most good.

## What's deferred to later modules

Species **interactions** -- how one species' presence or abundance relates to another's --
are covered in Module 6. **Temporal** patterns -- activity timing, seasonal shifts, and
predator-prey timing overlap -- are covered in Module 7.
